PullRequest.Title: Preserve terminal metadata in confirmation UI
PullRequest.Body:
This pull request focuses on preserving terminal metadata in the confirmation UI for terminal commands executed via the Copilot SDK. The changes ensure that the correct command and associated metadata are displayed in the confirmation window, addressing issues with previous implementations.

### Key Changes:
- **Preserved Terminal Metadata**: Ensured that terminal metadata is retained during the confirmation process, allowing the correct command to be displayed.
- **Approval Options Handling**: Updated the handling of approval options to ensure they are correctly reflected in the UI.
- **Cleaned Up Unnecessary Changes**: Removed unrelated changes and tests that were not necessary for the core functionality, streamlining the diff to focus on the essential updates.
- **Regression Tests**: Added tests to verify the correct display of terminal metadata and the functionality of all approval actions.

This update enhances the user experience by ensuring that the confirmation UI accurately reflects the command being executed, improving clarity and usability.

fixes #337337

Scenarios.Scenario: A tracked Copilot SDK tool reaches a normal permission prompt and is projected into the workbench confirmation UI.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The permission callback builds one pending_confirmation state, synchronously emits it, the host applies approval policy, and—when user input is required—the workbench renders the confirmation before the tool can continue. The new toToolCallMeta call is a shallow copy of the tracked metadata on this path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Transport one pending_confirmation protocol signal from the agent host to the workbench/approval side.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One signal per permission request that is not auto-approved; no collection fan-out or retry was added.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same pending_confirmation signal crossed the boundary; tracked calls omitted _meta, while untracked shell calls already sent a small terminal metadata object.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The signal must arrive before the confirmation can render or approval can resume the tool.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Cost scales with the number of permission prompts, not tool history. For terminal calls the tracked metadata created at tool start is normally two scalar fields (toolKind and language).
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Each tool call owns its own pending permission; concurrent tool calls can each prompt, but the diff adds neither a launcher nor aggregate concurrency and the UI carousel presents one active confirmation at a time when enabled.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is consulted or invalidated by the change. Metadata is read from the existing active-tool-call record and copied once for the event.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence in the event path and per-prompt cardinality from the changed emission and active-tool-call construction.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The prevalence of simultaneous permission prompts is unknown, but the added shallow object enumeration is bounded by the small typed metadata schema and occurs once per prompt.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: the diff preserves rendering metadata in an existing event without adding an expensive boundary, retry, or unbounded serialization.

Scenarios.Scenario: A custom bash or PowerShell command requests unsandboxed execution and waits for confirmation before process execution.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The shell tool invokes requestUnsandboxedCommandConfirmation, which emits one pending_confirmation event and waits for the user. Once approved, the existing shell-tool implementation may execute the command; the PR only attaches terminal metadata so the visible card is routed to the terminal renderer.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the unsandboxed pending-confirmation state to the host/workbench and return one approval decision.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One outbound prompt and one response per unsandboxed command request.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same prompt/response round-trip blocked execution; the event lacked terminal _meta.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Approval round-trip intentionally blocks command execution.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Execute the approved shell command through the existing custom shell tool.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one command execution for each approved request; denied requests launch none.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Approved commands followed the same execution path and count.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Execution is after the confirmation and is the command's primary work.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Cost scales one-for-one with unsandboxed command requests. The new metadata fallback computes a small tool-kind/language object once per request.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Concurrency remains whatever independent shell tool calls already permit; the PR does not add parallel requests or move subprocess launch before approval.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is added or bypassed. Session sandbox policy is read before and after approval exactly as before.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence: the callback wiring and await on pendingPermission establish ordering, and the changed line only enriches the existing signal.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Command duration and the number of concurrent prompts vary by workload, but neither is changed by this diff.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: no new subprocess, IPC round-trip, or critical-path await is introduced.

Scenarios.Scenario: The workbench renders a terminal confirmation with server-provided custom approval options, either inline or in the confirmation carousel, and the user selects one option.
Scenarios.CriticalPath: State adaptation maps the protocol options into confirmation messages; constructing the visible terminal card creates the existing pooled code editor and groups the option list into up to two buttons plus dropdown actions. Clicking an option sends one confirmation result. For sandbox-bypass cards, terminal metadata changes routing from the generic input card to the terminal card, but the generic input card also created a pooled code editor for the command payload.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Return the selected confirmation option identifier and kind to the agent-host session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Exactly one response for the selected action; dropdown construction does not issue boundary calls.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Generic custom-option confirmations already returned one selected option. This diff enables the same single response from the terminal-specific renderer.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The response resumes or rejects the pending tool call after user interaction.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Button construction is O(number of confirmation options), with the realistic changed scenario containing three options. Visible editor work is one card per active confirmation; carousel mode retains pending items but mounts the active content.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Inline mode can display existing concurrent prompts; carousel mode serializes visibility to one active item. The PR does not increase the number of prompts or editors generated by a request.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The editor pool is reused as before. No new cache keys or negative-cache behavior are introduced; button arrays are rebuilt only at card creation or existing auto-approve-action updates.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence in the O(n) grouping, pooled editor lifecycle, and single confirmation response from the changed constructor and click handler.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The protocol does not state a hard option-count cap, but repository producers/tests use small human-facing lists and there is no realistic evidence of a large collection.
Scenarios.Verdict: No reportable regression: the extracted grouping logic matches the previous generic implementation, realistic lists are small, and the terminal renderer replaces comparable visible editor work rather than adding repeated hidden work.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all six changed files and traced metadata serialization, confirmation rendering, option grouping, approval transport, and shell execution. The diff adds bounded per-prompt metadata/button work, no new expensive boundary calls, no fan-out or concurrency burst, and no cache or cleanup lifecycle regression. No findings were submitted.

Stats.CostNote: Copilot SDK reports nano-AI units and model billing multipliers; it does not provide a USD conversion.
